ety.text: From Middle English lone, lane, from Old Norse lán, from Proto-Germanic *laihną, from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ- (“to leave (over)”). Cognate with Icelandic lán, Swedish lån, Danish lån, German Lehen (“fief”), Dutch leen (“fief”), West Frisian lien, North Frisian leen (“fief; loan; office”), Scots lane, lain, len, Old English lǣn. More at lend.
From Scottish Gaelic lòn (“marshy meadow”) (compare lèana (“wet meadow, marsh, meadow”)).

senses.d: An act or instance of lending, an act or instance of granting something for temporary use.
ex: Because of the loan that John made to me, I was able to pay my tuition for the upcoming semester.

senses.d: A sum of money or other property that a natural or legal person borrows from another with the condition that it be returned or repaid over time or at a later date (sometimes with interest).
ex: All loans from the library, whether books or audio material, must be returned within two weeks.
He got a loan of five thousand pounds.

senses.d: The contract and array of legal or ethical obligations surrounding a loan.
ex: He made a payment on his loan.

senses.d: The permission to borrow any item.
ex: Thank you for the loan of your lawn mower.

senses.d: To lend (something) to (someone).
ex: All the rest—six out of eleven, more than half—were loaned to him.

senses.d: An area of uncultivated ground near a village or farmhouse.
ex: the Loan of Turchloy, the Black Loan
[...] The herds upon the loan, As if a sheep had fled, wi' speed, At Grumphy tykes hound on Wi' loud huzza!

ety.text: The sense of “burden” first arose in the 13th century as a secondary meaning of Middle English lode, loade, which had the main significance of “way, course, journey”, from Old English lād (“course, journey; way, street, waterway; leading, carrying; maintenance, support”) (ultimately from Proto-Germanic *laidō (“leading, way”), Proto-Indo-European *leyt- (“to go, go forth, die”). Cognate with Middle Low German leide (“entourage, escort”), German Leite (“line, course, load”), Swedish led (“way, trail, line”), Icelandic leið (“way, course, route”).
Acronym of living online all day.

senses.d: A burden; a weight to be carried.
ex: I struggled up the hill with the heavy load in my rucksack.

senses.d: A worry or concern to be endured, especially in the phrase a load off one's mind.
ex: Our life's a load.
I came here with a load and it feels so much lighter, now I’ve met you.

senses.d: A certain number of articles or quantity of material that can be transported or processed at one time.
ex: The truck overturned while carrying a full load of oil.
She put another load of clothes in the washing machine.

senses.d: A quantity of washing put into a washing machine for a wash cycle.
ex: I put a load on before we left.

senses.d: Used to form nouns that indicate a large quantity, often corresponding to the capacity of a vehicle
A large number or amount.
ex: I got loads of presents for my birthday!
I got a load of emails about that.

senses.d: The volume of work required to be performed.
ex: Will our web servers be able to cope with that load?

senses.d: The force exerted on a structural component such as a beam, girder, cable etc.
ex: Each of the cross-members must withstand a tensile load of 1,000 newtons.

senses.d: The electrical current or power delivered by a device.
ex: I'm worried that the load on that transformer will be too high.

senses.d: A resistive force encountered by a prime mover when performing work.
To put a load on or in (a means of conveyance or a place of storage).
ex: The dock workers refused to load the ship.

senses.d: To place in or on a conveyance or a place of storage.
ex: The longshoremen loaded the cargo quickly.
He loaded his stuff into his storage locker.

senses.d: To put a load on something.
ex: The truck was supposed to leave at dawn, but in fact we spent all morning loading.

senses.d: To receive a load.
ex: The truck is designed to load easily.
[I]n his Paroxyſms, as he vvalked the Streets, he vvould have his Pockets loaden vvith Stones, to pelt at the Signs.

senses.d: To be placed into storage or conveyance.
ex: The containers load quickly and easily.

senses.d: To fill (a firearm or artillery) with munition.
ex: I pulled the trigger, but nothing happened. I had forgotten to load the gun.

senses.d: To insert (an item or items) into an apparatus so as to ready it for operation, such as a reel of film into a camera, sheets of paper into a printer etc.
ex: Now that you've loaded the film [into the camera], you're ready to start shooting.
Now that you've loaded the camera [with film], you're ready to start shooting.

senses.d: To fill (an apparatus) with raw material.
ex: The workers loaded the blast furnace with coke and ore.

senses.d: To be put into use in an apparatus.
ex: The cartridge was designed to load easily.

senses.d: To read (data or a program) from a storage medium into computer memory.
ex: Click OK to load the selected data.

senses.d: A person that spends all day online. The term was originally used in the late 1980s to describe users on free Q-Link (later America Online) accounts who never signed off the system at great expense to the company.
ex: She never logs off; she is a real LOAD!

ex: Let’s leave the TV; the car is loaded already.

senses.d: Having a live round of ammunition in the chamber.
ex: No funny business; this heater’s loaded!

senses.d: Possessing great wealth.
ex: He sold his business a couple of years ago and is just loaded.
She told me that her Dad was loaded / I said “In that case, I’ll have rum and coca-cola”

senses.d: Drunk.
ex: By the end of the evening, the guests in the club were really loaded.

senses.d: Pertaining to a situation where there is a runner at each of the three bases.
ex: It's bottom of the ninth, the bases are loaded and there are two outs.

senses.d: Of a die or dice: weighted asymmetrically, and so biased to produce predictable throws.
ex: He was playing with loaded dice and won a fortune.

senses.d: Designed to produce a predictable answer, or to lay a trap.
ex: That interviewer is tricky; he asks loaded questions.

senses.d: Having strong connotations that colour the literal meaning and are likely to provoke an emotional response. Sometimes used loosely to describe a word that simply has many different meanings.
ex: "Ignorant" is a loaded word, often implying lack of intelligence rather than just lack of knowledge.

senses.d: Equipped with numerous options.
ex: She went all out; her new car is loaded.

senses.d: Covered with a topping or toppings; especially, covered with all available toppings that are offered as options for the dish.

ex: The position advertised a $40 per hour rate, inclusive of the casual loading.
